claims.text: Adding approximately 2 at% tungsten to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will produce thermally stable tungsten-rich precipitates.
The tungsten-rich precipitates will be located preferentially at grain boundaries.
Tungsten-rich precipitates will pin grain boundaries and inhibit grain-boundary movement.
Precipitate pinning will retard grain coarsening during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The tungsten addition will hinder high-temperature phase changes.
Microstructural stabilization that limits grain growth will limit degradation of microhardness and other mechanical properties.
The tungsten-doped alloy will preserve or enhance elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the undoped alloy.
The initial titanium- and nickel-primary alloy has a predominantly BCC solid solution with possible secondary phases.
Aging at approximately 1000 °C for about 100 hours in argon is an applicable high-temperature test condition.
After the specified anneal, the tungsten-doped alloy will exhibit significantly less grain growth than the undoped alloy.
After the specified anneal, the tungsten-doped alloy will exhibit a smaller decrease in Vickers microhardness than the undoped alloy.
The proposed effect applies when tungsten content does not exceed roughly 2 at%.
Diffusion-controlled grain growth is dominant under the specified operating conditions.
Precipitate pinning is a known grain-refinement mechanism in many alloys.
Processing conditions and phase stability may alter the effectiveness of the proposed intervention.
